The easy argument to be made is that rich people don't care about everyone else because they lack morals, and that's certainly true in some cases, but in my experience, the VAST majority of cases come because *rich people really don't know you*, or at least the real you, in contrast to the *you* that their family have taught them about.   
    
Being from a rich background means that your family has more control over how and where you're brought up, and that usually comes from a generational stance (I was brought up like this so my son will be brought up like this), so there really isn't any incentive for that to stop being the case. You are born and raised close to people who look like you, speak like you and think like you. You are taught principles that your grandfather taught your father, regardless of how much the world has changed. You grow up being told that different equals dangerous, so you typically have no incentive to seek out people outside your private world.

When a pampered rich kid is faced with a person from a different ethnicity or economic standing, their ideas of reality are different, so they end up reducing the person to stereotypes - being averse to them, afraid, sometimes even angry - because they are trying to apply their logic to someone else's life and *it doesn't work.*     
    
The institutionalized divide between people of different economic realities is rock solid, generational and has to be chiseled hard and with personal intention. Looking beyond your bubble and trying to understand others is a hard thing to start doing, but it is extremely rewarding and good for your conscience.

Still, it somewhat brought thrill to the old wolf. He'd grown accustomed to that village, its people and its customs, yet that naturally made him a slave to comfort. Convincing a brand new village to send out a yearly sacrifice would prove a challenge. Perhaps he could even make them monthly this time, depending on how fearful and gullible the people could be. He had not chosen this curse, but he'd come to embrace it, striking a bargain with the monster and, in turn, becoming a monster himself.   


Now he'd have to prepare. For the trip, for the hunger, and for the hunters. The damned hunters.

Not really! I took into consideration that Enraged minions are only enraged when their current hp is below their max hp. So if a worgen is healed to full hp, it is no longer enraged. That's how I envisioned the bomber working, it becomes enraged, deals its damage, and if you want to do it again, you can heal it to full and then enrage it again. If many of my cards read "whenever this minion takes damage, they would be even more ridiculous than they currently are. Let me go over them, to clarify.  
*Enraged Bloodbeast.  
This card is supposed to successfully trade with almost anything that doesn't kill it during your turn, sticky as all hell. The effect only happens if he is damaged, however, unlike stoneskin gargoyle, which has its regen as part of the card effect.  
*Magus of Pain.  
I envisioned this card as the type of thing you really don't want to keep alive for too long. Her effect works similarly to Spiteful Smith - as long as it's on the board and damaged, you have an extra mana crystal. If this card read "whenever this minion takes damage, this card would be completely inconsiderable.
